The Eastern fence lizard (Sceloporus undulatus) deposits leathery-shelled eggs in shallow nests during late spring. Incubation proceeds at soil temperatures that often stabilize near 28 °C [T = 28 °C]; under such thermal conditions, the period from oviposition to hatching spans approximately 62 days [ab = approximately 62 days]. This incubation interval is consistent with the extended embryonic development typical of temperate-zone iguanian lizards, where ambient thermal regimes govern the rate of blastula formation and subsequent organogenesis. Hatchlings escape the egg by means of a transient egg caruncle, a structure used to perforate the parchment-like shell in the behavior known as shell pipping. At emergence, neonatal body mass averages 0.56 g [Wwb = 0.56 g], while snout–vent length is approximately 2.5 cm [Lb = approximately 2.5 cm]. The small hatchling mass reflects the finite yolk endowment provided during vitellogenesis, leaving neonates dependent on prompt exotrophic feeding. Within hours of eclosion, the yolk-sac larva absorbs remaining internal yolk, transitioning to active foraging on small arthropods—a critical phase that largely determines early juvenile survival. Field observations indicate that mortality during this exotrophic transition can exceed fifty percent in some populations, a pattern that underscores the vulnerability of the hatchling size phenotype.

As growth proceeds, juvenile S. undulatus undergo a phase of rapid mass gain, eventually reaching an asymptotic adult body size. In long-term field studies and captive rearing experiments, the ultimate snout–vent length (SVL) recorded for adult individuals reaches approximately 8 cm [Li = approximately 8 cm], with a corresponding ultimate wet body mass of about 18 g [Wwi = about 18 g]. This adult size is broadly comparable to that of congeneric Sceloporus species inhabiting similar temperate woodland habitats, although local resource availability and predation pressure can generate measurable geographic variation. The attainment of maximum structural size is typically decoupled from the completion of body mass accumulation; individuals often reach near-final SVL earlier, with subsequent somatic investment directed toward body condition and fat storage. Adult females tend to have slightly larger body masses than males when gravid, but non-gravid mass dimorphism is modest in this species. The 18-gram adult mass represents the culmination of multiple years of growth under favorable conditions, with individuals in lower-quality habitats seldom exceeding 15 grams. These ontogenetic patterns, documented through mark–recapture studies, illustrate the interplay between genetic growth potential and environmental constraints on realized adult size.

In S. undulatus, the onset of sexual maturation occurs well before the attainment of maximum adult size, a pattern widespread among squamate reptiles. Field dissection studies reveal that gonadal activation and the initiation of gametogenesis are associated with a threshold structural size. Specifically, individuals typically reach puberty at a snout–vent length of approximately 5.8 cm [Lp = approximately 5.8 cm], at which point body mass averages about 6.9 g [Wwp = about 6.9 g]. This pubertal mass represents only about 38% of the asymptotic adult body mass, indicating that reproductive physiology becomes functional while substantial somatic growth remains to be completed. The decoupling of sexual maturation from final body size is thought to permit earlier breeding under favorable environmental conditions, a bet-hedging strategy in habitats with uncertain resource pulses. Histological examination of gonadal tissues in sub-adult lizards confirms that spermatogenesis and ovarian follicle development coincide with these size thresholds, enabling first reproductive attempts at an age of less than one year in warm-climate populations. In cooler upland populations, pubertal SVL may be slightly larger—closer to 6.3 cm—presumably reflecting a longer juvenile growth period necessitated by lower ambient temperatures. Moreover, the age at which individuals attain the 5.8 cm length threshold varies interannually: spring-hatched lizards often reach puberty by late summer, whereas late-summer hatchlings frequently overwinter as immatures and mature only the following spring. These patterns align with life-history models predicting that early maturation is advantageous only when juvenile growth rates permit sexual development within a single activity season, a condition met in low-elevation, warm environments.

Quantitative assessments of reproductive output in the Eastern fence lizard have been conducted under controlled thermal regimes to isolate the effects of temperature on clutch production. At a constant ambient temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], gravid females reliably produce multiple clutches throughout the active season. Detailed nesting records indicate that individual females produce an average of 8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 8 eggs per clutch], a clutch size that appears optimal for balancing maternal investment with offspring size. More strikingly, under these favorable thermal conditions, individual females can produce as many as 5 clutches annually [F_R_i = 5 clutches annually], a frequency that places S. undulatus among the more fecund members of the genus. This reproductive schedule means that a female may deposit roughly 40 eggs in a single breeding season, a level of output that likely evolved in response to high nest and juvenile mortality rates typical of their open-woodland and edge habitats. The sensitivity of vitellogenesis and egg shelling to ambient temperature is well documented in this species, with clutch frequency declining markedly when mean temperatures fall below 22 °C. In field enclosures where thermal regimes were manipulated via shade treatments, clutch frequency fell to only 2–3 per year in cooler plots, confirming the strong dependence of egg production on thermal opportunity. The inter-clutch interval, typically 20–25 days under optimal conditions, lengthens noticeably when ambient temperatures drop, reducing total seasonal fecundity. Despite this temperature sensitivity, the species maintains a wide latitudinal distribution, suggesting that local adaptations in reproductive phenology compensate for climatic variation. In northern populations, the breeding season is compressed, and females usually produce only two or three clutches per year, whereas southern populations may sustain the five-clutch rate.

The pace of life in S. undulatus is notably rapid, with individuals moving from hatching to first breeding within a single growing season under warm conditions. Experimental rearing at a constant 28.9 °C [T = 28.9 °C] has shown that first reproduction can be achieved as early as 152.5 days after hatching [tR = 152.5 days after hatching], a developmental trajectory that allows hatchlings from early-season clutches to themselves reproduce before the onset of winter. This early age at first breeding is a pivotal life-history trait, enabling high population growth rates in habitats with prolonged warm periods. By contrast, the maximum lifespan of this species remains modest even under optimal captive care. Individuals maintained at 24 °C [T = 24 °C] have survived up to 2,790 days [am = up to 2,790 days], equivalent to roughly 7.6 years. Such longevity, while substantial for a small phrynosomatid, is seldom realized in the wild, where predation, disease, and winter mortality typically limit survival to three or four years. The combination of rapid maturation, high reproductive output, and a moderate adult lifespan characterizes S. undulatus as a classic r-selected ectotherm adapted to disturbance-prone environments. This suite of traits places the Eastern fence lizard on the opportunistic end of the life-history continuum within the Phrynosomatidae, contrasting with slower-maturing, long-lived species such as Horned Lizards (Phrynosoma). The rapid turnover of generations facilitates swift colonization of disturbed patches, a key factor in the species' success across anthropogenic landscapes. Long-term population studies suggest that annual adult survival rates average 30–40%, with most individuals dying within their first three years, a pattern consistent with the observed maximum longevity of about 7.6 years under protected conditions.
